*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: Research/Engineering/Performance.md
@@
 ## Research-compute specific opportunities
@@
 - Record hardware, versions, seeds, wall time, peak memory, and numerical differences.
+
+## Complexity and bottleneck example
+
+Suppose a naive feature builder recomputes a 60-day rolling statistic for every date from all prior rows, causing work to grow roughly quadratically with sample length. A rolling update can maintain a sum/sum-of-squares or use a tested rolling kernel, reducing repeated work toward linear time. For numerically stable variance, prefer a robust online algorithm or validated library rather than subtracting two nearly equal large quantities without checking error.
+
+Profile representative data, not a toy slice that omits I/O or memory pressure. Record wall-clock time, CPU, peak resident memory, I/O volume, and output equivalence. Optimization that changes missing-value, timestamp, or floating-point behavior can change a backtest result; compare outputs with domain-specific tolerances and rerun leakage/data-quality assertions.
+
+## Parallelism and determinism
+
+Parallelize independent instruments, folds, or parameter batches only when results are independent and resource-bounded. Nested BLAS/OpenMP, process pools, and GPU workers can oversubscribe cores and memory. Set thread limits, pin seeds where meaningful, preserve deterministic task IDs, and aggregate outputs in stable order. Floating-point reductions can vary with parallel execution order; quantify acceptable numerical variation.
+
+## Cache invalidation
+
+A cache key should include source snapshot/version, query parameters, transformation code digest, schema, calendar, and relevant environment settings. A cache that omits vintage or universe version can silently reuse stale or hindsight-adjusted data. Cache only deterministic transforms; record whether the value was fetched or recomputed.
*** Update File: Research/Engineering/Research pipeline architecture.md
@@
 ## Failure policy
@@
 - Preserve raw input before attempting repair. Record any repair as a derived transformation.
+
+## Idempotency and recovery example
+
+For a paginated daily feed, define a partition key (provider, product, instrument, date range, query version) and a deterministic page/cursor record. Write each page to a temporary object, validate response status/schema and expected cursor progression, then atomically commit it with row count/checksum/status. On retry, resume from the last committed cursor; do not append the same page twice. A missing page is an incomplete partition, not an empty period.
+
+## Data contracts at stage boundaries
+
+Each pipeline boundary should state schema, primary key, sort order, timestamp/availability semantics, unit/currency, null policy, and invariants. Validate contract before and after transformations. Preserve quarantine rows and exception disposition, since silent “cleaning” can selectively remove crashes, illiquid instruments, or failed issuers.
+
+## Reproducibility versus reproducible access
+
+If raw data cannot be retained under terms, the run may not be snapshot-reproducible. Preserve compliant query metadata, source version, retrieval timestamp, field dictionary, license reference, response hash if permitted, and a concise note that re-query may return revised data. State the attained reproducibility level using [[Experiment reproducibility]].
*** Update File: Research/Engineering/Data validation patterns.md
@@
 Pandera is one Python library for declaring dataframe schemas and checks. Schema tools enforce coded rules; the research team remains responsible for choosing valid rules and data semantics.
+
+## Severity and quarantine policy
+
+Classify checks as hard failures (e.g., malformed schema, sequence gap that invalidates book state), warnings (e.g., unusual but plausible return), or informational diagnostics (e.g., source update count). A warning should not automatically drop observations. Store raw input, rule/version, row key, observed value, and disposition. Exceptions should be explicit and reviewable; never define an “invalid” threshold by whether the row hurts strategy performance.
+
+## Cross-source reconciliation example
+
+For a sample of liquid contracts, align venue, contract code, timestamp, price type, and units before comparing values. Estimate difference distributions and investigate systematic offsets, session mismatches, stale marks, and corporate/roll adjustments. Agreement does not prove either source is correct; it only bounds certain discrepancies. For official macro values, compare release/vintage and seasonal-adjustment status rather than only matching reference dates.
+
+## Monitoring drift in data itself
+
+Track coverage, missingness, duplicate rate, quote age, latency, symbol counts, unit distributions, schema/version changes, and cross-source residuals by time. A sudden feature distribution shift may be an economic regime change or a collection pipeline change; join diagnostics to provider notices and source metadata before attributing it to markets.
*** Update File: Research/Engineering/Experiment reproducibility.md
@@
 Research claims should state which level was achieved. Prospective testing does not automatically imply broad external validity.
+
+## Determinism and numerical reproducibility
+
+Exact bitwise reproduction may be impossible across hardware, BLAS libraries, GPU kernels, parallel reduction order, or nondeterministic algorithms. State whether the goal is bitwise identity, metric agreement within a tolerance, or conceptual replication. Record package/runtime/hardware, deterministic settings, seeds, and tolerances. A seed alone does not guarantee repeatability when code, library versions, data ordering, or distributed execution differ.
+
+## Artifact and report contract
+
+Keep a compact report with hypothesis, estimand, source/vintage, universe, split and selection protocol, baseline, net-cost assumptions, uncertainty, results by time/regime, diagnostics, limitations, and next falsification. Link tables/plots to their run ID and data/code digest; do not publish screenshots without the underlying computation metadata. Preserve negative and failed runs as part of the reproducibility record.
*** Update File: Research/Engineering/Experiment tracking implementation notes.md
@@
 See [[Experiment reproducibility]] and [[Research pipeline architecture]].
+
+## Trial taxonomy

# Translating Economics into Market Hypotheses

2. **Observable proxy:** identify data that measures the mechanism, including its error and release process.
3. **Information time:** specify when each observation was public and when prices could react.
4. **Market mapping:** define instruments exposed to the mechanism, with direction and horizon.
5. **Competing explanation:** risk premium, broad factor, seasonality, liquidity, or reverse causality.
6. **Empirical design:** event study, panel/time series, cross-sectional comparison, causal design, or predictive test.
7. **Trading translation:** costs, execution, constraints, sizing, capacity, and risk.
8. **Validation:** chronological holdout, independent source/market test, robustness, and decay monitoring.

## Macro data require real-time vintages

Macroeconomic series are revised and often published after the reference period. Forecasting with final revised values can create look-ahead bias. Store release timestamps, original values, revisions, consensus expectations, and surprise definitions separately. The timestamp when a number is known is distinct from the period it describes.

## Regime dependence is testable, not a free explanation

display.text:
# Translating Economics into Market Hypotheses

Economic theories describe incentives, constraints, equilibrium, and adjustment. A market hypothesis requires a measurable implication with clear timing, a tradable instrument, and a method that can distinguish competing explanations.

## Translation chain

1. **Economic mechanism:** e.g. a supply constraint, inventory adjustment, policy surprise, financing constraint, or information delay.
2. **Observable proxy:** identify data that measures the mechanism, including its error and release process.
3. **Information time:** specify when each observation was public and when prices could react.
4. **Market mapping:** define instruments exposed to the mechanism, with direction and horizon.
5. **Competing explanation:** risk premium, broad factor, seasonality, liquidity, or reverse causality.
6. **Empirical design:** event study, panel/time series, cross-sectional comparison, causal design, or predictive test.
7. **Trading translation:** costs, execution, constraints, sizing, capacity, and risk.
8. **Validation:** chronological holdout, independent source/market test, robustness, and decay monitoring.

## Macro data require real-time vintages

Macroeconomic series are revised and often published after the reference period. Forecasting with final revised values can create look-ahead bias. Store release timestamps, original values, revisions, consensus expectations, and surprise definitions separately. The timestamp when a number is known is distinct from the period it describes.

## Regime dependence is testable, not a free explanation

If a proposed relationship only works in recessions, high-volatility periods, or a specific policy regime, define that condition ex ante and estimate uncertainty within it. Avoid searching thresholds after observing returns. The regime may itself be measured with future-revised data or subject to classification error.

## Example: fiscal news to rates / FX

Possible mechanism: an unexpected change in fiscal outlook shifts expected issuance, demand, inflation, or policy reaction. Candidate data include release-time budget documents, auction results, real-time forecasts, yields, inflation expectations, and exchange rates. Design must distinguish fiscal news from simultaneous economic news, global risk, central-bank expectations, and pre-announcement pricing. A yield/FX response is not automatically a profitable strategy; assess transaction costs, event timing, and cross-country variation.

## Example: physical supply data to futures

Possible mechanism: a transport bottleneck changes expected regional inventory and near-term convenience yield. Use timestamped shipping, weather, port, production, and inventory releases; map route/grade/location to contracts and calendar spreads. Test whether data arrival precedes price movement and whether it adds value over public reports, seasonality, and known inventory releases.

# Regime Stability and Forecast Comparison Exercise

This exercise examines whether a forecast adds stable information beyond simple baselines. It is educational and does not assert a profitable strategy.

## Question

Does one forecasting model consistently improve on a naive baseline across chronological test windows, and does any apparent gain depend on a particular volatility/regime period?

## Design

1. Select one liquid instrument/series and a point-in-time-safe target (e.g. next-period return or realized volatility).
2. Choose one simple benchmark and one candidate model before reviewing final results.
3. Use rolling-origin evaluation; define training window, refit cadence, horizon, and any label-overlap handling.
4. Score with a loss appropriate to the target. For returns, separate forecast loss from portfolio/decision utility; for variance forecasts, consider QLIKE and calibration.
5. Store each forecast, origin time, data vintage, model fit window, and realization.
6. Plot the loss differential and calibration over time; summarize by pre-defined volatility regimes or calendar subperiods.
7. If comparing models formally, use inference appropriate to serial correlation and overlapping horizons; do not treat each forecast origin as iid.
8. Record all model variants and avoid using the final evaluation window to tune the specification.

## Questions to answer

display.text:
# Regime Stability and Forecast Comparison Exercise

This exercise examines whether a forecast adds stable information beyond simple baselines. It is educational and does not assert a profitable strategy.

## Question

Does one forecasting model consistently improve on a naive baseline across chronological test windows, and does any apparent gain depend on a particular volatility/regime period?

## Design

1. Select one liquid instrument/series and a point-in-time-safe target (e.g. next-period return or realized volatility).
2. Choose one simple benchmark and one candidate model before reviewing final results.
3. Use rolling-origin evaluation; define training window, refit cadence, horizon, and any label-overlap handling.
4. Score with a loss appropriate to the target. For returns, separate forecast loss from portfolio/decision utility; for variance forecasts, consider QLIKE and calibration.
5. Store each forecast, origin time, data vintage, model fit window, and realization.
6. Plot the loss differential and calibration over time; summarize by pre-defined volatility regimes or calendar subperiods.
7. If comparing models formally, use inference appropriate to serial correlation and overlapping horizons; do not treat each forecast origin as iid.
8. Record all model variants and avoid using the final evaluation window to tune the specification.

## Questions to answer

- Is average improvement concentrated in one episode or regime?
- How large is the uncertainty interval around the loss difference?
- Are model wins robust to an economically equivalent loss and alternative baseline?
- Does any forecast advantage improve net decision utility after realistic costs?
- Is the regime label available in real time, or defined using future/full-sample information?
- What was the total search space, including targets, horizons, models, windows, and scoring rules?

## Write-up

Include pre-specified design, data source and vintage, forecast origins, baselines, loss definition, dependence handling, per-window results, calibration, costs if translated to a trade, and limitations. Append a timestamped entry to [[log]].

# . . . and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns

## Bibliography

- **Authors:** Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu, Heqing Zhu
- **Date / version:** NBER Working Paper, October 2014; published in *Review of Financial Studies* 29(1), 2016, pp. 5–68.
- **DOI:** [10.1093/rfs/hhv059](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhv059)
- **Primary abstract / working paper:** [NBER Working Paper 20592](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20592)
- **Open full text:** NBER working paper landing page links a PDF; access and reuse terms are set by NBER/publisher. Not copied locally.

## Assessment

- **Evidence grade:** 2 — published peer-reviewed financial-economics methods paper, foundational for factor discovery discussion; publication age is a caveat for current factor counts and thresholds.
- **Recency:** 2016 publication; foundational, but pair with newer replication and methodological work.
- **Novelty:** High historical significance for the multiple-testing debate, though now widely cited.
- **Source type:** Peer-reviewed journal article; NBER working paper version.
- **Claim evaluated:** The scale of factor mining makes conventional significance thresholds inadequate; the paper proposes a framework that allows correlated tests and missing data and estimates higher hurdles for newly discovered factors.

## Summary

The authors study the large number of proposed factors in the cross-section of expected returns. Because researchers have tried many characteristics and specifications, a conventional single-test t-statistic threshold can produce false discoveries. Their framework estimates time-varying significance cutoffs while allowing dependence among tests and missing observations. The paper argues that new factors should face a substantially higher bar than the traditional `t > 2` convention.

## Limitations and research use

- The exact numerical hurdle depends on assumptions about the historical discovery process and effective trial count; do not convert it into a universal rule for every strategy class or sample.
- Factor literature is a specific setting; strategy search, intraday data, and non-equity signals have different dependence structures.
- Use it to motivate complete search logs, multiplicity-aware inference, and caution with reported novelty—not as a substitute for independent validation.

- **Author:** Robert Novy-Marx
- **Date / version:** NBER Working Paper 21329, July 2015.

- **Primary source:** [NBER Working Paper 21329](https://www.nber.org/papers/w21329)

## Assessment

- **Recency:** 2015; foundational warning, but complement with newer methods and current empirical replications.
- **Novelty:** Important demonstration that selecting/composing signals compounds selection bias.
- **Source type:** NBER working paper.

## Summary

The paper analyzes how multi-signal strategies can look highly significant even when their candidate signals have no genuine predictive power. If signals are oriented/selected to have positive in-sample association, choosing combinations introduces large biases. The paper derives and examines t-statistic behavior and emphasizes that signal selection amplifies multiple-testing bias.

## Limitations and research use

- The result addresses a specific signal-selection/composition problem; it is not a universal correction for all strategies.

- **Recency:** 2017; well-established, but market regimes and practical cost assumptions evolve.
- **Novelty:** Demonstrates dynamic risk scaling as a portfolio-construction dimension across multiple factors and currency carry.
- **Source type:** Peer-reviewed journal article / NBER working paper.

## Summary

The paper studies scaling exposure down when realized volatility is high. The authors report improved Sharpe ratios and utility for several equity factors and currency carry, arguing that factor expected returns do not rise proportionally with volatility. # Comparing Predictive Accuracy

## Bibliography

- **Authors:** Francis X. Diebold and Roberto S. Mariano
- **Date / version:** NBER Technical Working Paper 0169, November 1994; published in *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics* 13 (1995), pp. 253–265.
- **DOI:** [10.3386/t0169](https://doi.org/10.3386/t0169)
- **Source:** [NBER Working Paper T0169](https://www.nber.org/papers/t0169)

## Assessment

- **Evidence grade:** 2 — foundational scholarly forecasting methodology paper; its application requires correct loss, dependence, and model-selection treatment.
- **Recency:** 1995; still a central reference, but pair with later refinements and current forecast-design literature.
- **Source type:** Published academic paper / NBER technical working paper.

## Summary and use

The Diebold–Mariano approach compares forecast accuracy by examining a time series of loss differentials between two forecasts and testing whether the expected differential is zero. Serial dependence in the loss differential is important, particularly with multi-step or overlapping forecast horizons.

## Caveats

- The test does not correct for broad model search or repeated holdout use.
- Test conclusions depend on forecast origins, loss function, horizon, and long-run variance estimation.
- Equal predictive accuracy is distinct from equal trading utility; implementability and transaction costs require separate evaluation.

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: Research/Sources/Harvey Liu Zhu 2016.md
@@
 ## Limitations and research use
@@
 - Use it to motivate complete search logs, multiplicity-aware inference, and caution with reported novelty—not as a substitute for independent validation.
+
+## Reading the result carefully
+
+The paper is about discovery thresholds in a literature where candidate factors accumulate over time. Its central lesson is selection-aware: the nominal significance level for a single pre-specified test does not describe the evidence in a large, adaptive factor search. The proposed hurdle depends on assumptions about the trial process and dependence among tests. Use the framework as a prompt to reconstruct what was searched and to ask which discoveries are genuinely independent; do not transplant a headline t-statistic threshold to unrelated intraday or alternative-data searches.
+
+## Practical translation
+
+For an internal strategy project, enumerate the actual search dimensions (markets, horizons, features, costs, universes, transforms, model classes, stopping decisions). A complete experiment history may be more actionable than trying to infer an effective number of tests from a final result alone. Pair multiplicity treatment with point-in-time validation, dependence-aware uncertainty, and independent confirmation.
*** Update File: Research/Sources/Novy-Marx 2015.md
@@
 ## Limitations and research use
@@
 - Pair with [[Harvey Liu Zhu 2016]] and [[Overfitting controls]].
+
+## Mechanism of the bias
+
+If each noisy signal is oriented or retained because it looked favorable in the same sample, the retained signals have positive estimation error conditional on selection. Combining them does not restore independence from that selection; it can make the resulting strategy appear more precise than the underlying evidence warrants. This is a research-process issue, not a property unique to machine learning.
+
+## Practical translation
+
+Freeze signal definitions and orientation on development data, record all candidate signals (including discarded ones), and evaluate the fixed combination procedure on untouched chronological data. If weights or signs are learned, that learning belongs inside the training/nested validation process. The paper's results motivate selection controls but do not provide a universal correction for every correlated signal family.
*** Update File: Research/Sources/Athey Imbens 2017.md
@@
 ## Research use and caveat
@@
 Financial prediction is often not a causal question. However, causal reasoning helps assess mechanism, confounding, event studies, and whether an apparent relationship is plausibly transportable. Markets can respond to anticipation, simultaneity, and changing equilibrium, so policy-evaluation designs require careful adaptation.
+
+## How to use this review
+
+Treat it as a map of applied causal-inference design choices, not as a recipe that makes observational data causal. For any method, identify its estimand and identifying assumption (e.g. continuity near a regression-discontinuity cutoff or parallel trends for difference-in-differences). Modern ML can help estimate nuisance functions or heterogeneity, but cannot manufacture exogenous treatment assignment. In financial settings, market anticipation, interference across firms/instruments, and equilibrium responses make the counterfactual especially substantive.
*** Update File: Research/Sources/Moreira Muir 2017.md
@@
 ## Research use and limitations
@@
 - Study subsequent critiques, replications, and live implementability before relying on the reported improvement.
+
+## Replication design
+
+Separate the question “does scaling alter risk-adjusted portfolio outcomes?” from “does a volatility forecast predict returns?” Recreate the original portfolio and scaling rule as closely as permitted, then test a frozen implementation with lagged forecasts, leverage bounds, turnover, costs, and chronological evaluation. Compare fixed exposure, volatility-targeted exposure, and a simple risk control under identical dates. Report return, volatility, drawdown/tails, exposures, and turnover so improved Sharpe is not mistaken for higher alpha.
*** Update File: Research/Sources/Bacry Mastromatteo Muzy 2015.md
@@
 ## Research use and caveats
@@
 Event clustering can reflect endogenous excitation, common exogenous news, or measurement/venue effects; a fitted self-excitation parameter is not automatically causal. Check stationarity/stability, timestamp quality, omitted common shocks, kernel choice, sampling, and out-of-sample calibration. Tick-level model fit does not establish exploitable net alpha.
+
+## Minimal model interpretation
+
+A univariate Hawkes process has conditional intensity \(\lambda(t)=\mu+\sum_{t_i<t}g(t-t_i)\), where \(\mu\) is baseline intensity and \(g\) captures excitation after earlier events. A multivariate model adds cross-event kernels. The kernels describe conditional arrival clustering under the specified model; they do not identify whether the cause is strategic reaction, common news, or omitted state variables. Compare against a time-of-day baseline and include exogenous covariates before interpreting excitation.
*** Update File: Research/Sources/Diebold Mariano 1995.md
@@
 ## Caveats
@@
 - Equal predictive accuracy is distinct from equal trading utility; implementability and transaction costs require separate evaluation.
+
+## Loss-differential interpretation
+
+Given forecasts A and B, define \(d_t=L(e_{A,t})-L(e_{B,t})\) under one predeclared loss. A negative mean favors A in the evaluation sample. The test standardizes that mean by an estimate of the long-run variance of \(d_t\), so serial dependence matters. The test asks about expected predictive loss under the specified design; it neither selects a loss for the researcher nor resolves broad model search, nonstationarity, or whether the forecast changes net decisions.
*** End Patch

+## Reading the result carefully
+
+The paper is about discovery thresholds in a literature where candidate factors accumulate over time. Its central lesson is selection-aware: the nominal significance level for a single pre-specified test does not describe the evidence in a large, adaptive factor search. The proposed hurdle depends on assumptions about the trial process and dependence among tests. Use the framework as a prompt to reconstruct what was searched and to ask which discoveries are genuinely independent; do not transplant a headline t-statistic threshold to unrelated intraday or alternative-data searches.
+
+## Practical translation
+
+For an internal strategy project, enumerate the actual search dimensions (markets, horizons, features, costs, universes, transforms, model classes, stopping decisions). A complete experiment history may be more actionable than trying to infer an effective number of tests from a final result alone. Pair multiplicity treatment with point-in-time validation, dependence-aware uncertainty, and independent confirmation.

 - Pair with [[Harvey Liu Zhu 2016]] and [[Overfitting controls]].
 
+## Mechanism of the bias
+
+If each noisy signal is oriented or retained because it looked favorable in the same sample, the retained signals have positive estimation error conditional on selection. Combining them does not restore independence from that selection; it can make the resulting strategy appear more precise than the underlying evidence warrants. This is a research-process issue, not a property unique to machine learning.
+
+## Practical translation
+
+Freeze signal definitions and orientation on development data, record all candidate signals (including discarded ones), and evaluate the fixed combination procedure on untouched chronological data. If weights or signs are learned, that learning belongs inside the training/nested validation process. The paper's results motivate selection controls but do not provide a universal correction for every correlated signal family.

# Quantitative Research Obsidian Vault — Plan

> **Vault folder:** `Research` (Obsidian vault name: `research`)

## Purpose

Build a deep, linked educational and research vault for interns learning to develop, research, and test ideas. The broad scope includes economics and quantitative methods, with the primary emphasis on quantifying data, identifying statistically credible market edges, and understanding how edges may decay.

Collect a wide range of material, including less conventional or obscure leads. Preserve the distinction between a novel hypothesis and evidence that supports it: unusual correlations may inspire research, but must be labeled and tested rather than presented as established alpha.

## Source and evidence policy

- Search broadly across academic research, textbooks, lecture notes, technical writing, datasets, and documented practitioner accounts.
- Classify source claims on a **1–10 evidence/provenance scale** (lower is stronger). Grade 1 is a recent, reputable peer-reviewed/academic or primary-source item with transparent methodology, accessible provenance, and independently checkable evidence. Grades 2–3 are strong academic/official sources with minor caveats or early-stage status; grades 4–6 are useful but more limited, older, indirect, or methodologically incomplete; grades 7–8 are trade/practitioner and secondary material with partial verification; grades 9–10 are anecdotal stories, opaque claims, or unverified leads. The grade applies to the source's support for a specific claim, not to whether the idea deserves exploration.
- Keep **evidence grade**, **recency**, and **novelty** as separate fields. A dated foundational result may remain high-quality evidence; a recent vendor claim is not high-quality evidence simply because it is current.
- Record publication/update date, author or institution, source type, methods, limitations, and a direct link wherever available.
- Treat recency and reliability as separate considerations: an older foundational result can remain valuable, and a recent anecdote is not strong evidence merely because it is recent.
- Summarize and link copyrighted works. Include local copies only when distribution is permitted. Flag useful works that require the user to provide a copy.
- Include a practical London Strategic Edge data-source walkthrough, verifying access requirements, dependencies, data formats, quotas, and workflow against current official documentation and repository source.

## Vault structure

Create a navigable `index.md` and a running `log.md`, then organize substantial subject areas into linked topic notes and subtopics. Keep market-specific material in dedicated folders and cross-link it to shared methods and concepts.

### Core areas to cover

- Mathematics: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, probability, statistics, optimization, and multidimensional geometry/topology.
- Econometrics and economics: time series, causal inference, forecasting, market and macroeconomic data, and empirical methods.
- Machine learning: supervised and unsupervised learning, deep learning, LSTMs and sequence methods, reinforcement learning, and applications to financial data.
- Research practice: data quality, feature construction, backtesting, validation, multiple testing, leakage, overfitting prevention, statistical significance, robustness, and edge decay.
- Engineering: efficient data workflows, profiling, runtime reduction, code execution and numerical optimization, reproducibility, and research pipelines.
- Data and alternative hypotheses: document provenance, transformations, limitations, and evidence quality; retain unconventional leads with clear uncertainty labels.

### Market folders

Create dedicated folders for at least:

- Forex
- ETFs
- Crypto
- Equities
- Futures
- Options
- Fixed income
- Commodities

Add further markets when useful. Each market area should cover relevant data, instruments, market structure, research considerations, and links to shared methods.

## Progress checklist

### Planning and structure

- [x] Capture the vault goals and scope.
- [x] Define source/evidence grading principles and copyright handling.
- [x] Specify the index, research log, and linked-note organization.
- [x] Specify market-specific folders.
- [x] Agree on a working source-grade rubric (1 strongest to 10 weakest; evidence, recency, and novelty recorded separately).
- [x] Create the folder structure and starter navigation files inside the `Research` vault.
- [x] Create `index.md`, `log.md`, shared topic folders, and dedicated folders/notes for Forex, ETFs, Crypto, Equities, Futures, Options, Fixed Income, and Commodities.

### Research and content

- [x] Inventory core topics and build an initial linked curriculum map.
- [x] Research and document London Strategic Edge, including dependencies and a step-by-step data-use walkthrough.
- [x] Collect and grade an initial group of sources across quantitative methods, ML, finance, research engineering, and data.
- [x] Develop first-pass topic notes and subtopic notes with summaries, links, limitations, and cross-links.
- [x] Expand edge-validation material with inferential pitfalls, alternative-data design, economics-to-market mapping, exercises, and additional academic research leads.
- [x] Add a microstructure/high-frequency research pass covering book reconstruction, execution costs, event models, and source-grounded exercises.
- [x] Add a primary financial/economic data-source directory and detailed point-in-time, vintage, identifier, revision, and access guidance.
- [x] Add an alternative-data opportunity map, physical-supply-chain case study, source notes, and an evaluation checklist.
- [x] Add practical ingestion architecture, schema validation, experiment tracking, and reproducibility guidance.
- [x] Deepen time-series research with forecast comparison, structural instability, volatility forecasting, and a practical stability exercise.
- [x] Add an options-market research pass on implied volatility, variance risk premia, VIX, data limitations, and a forecast-to-trading exercise.
- [x] Deepen existing statistical inference, forecast evaluation, probability, overfitting, and financial ML validation notes with derivations and worked examples.
- [ ] Expand each first-pass topic with deeper derivations, worked examples, datasets, research exercises, and additional high-quality/obscure source leads.
- [ ] Populate market folders with market-specific data and research material.
- [ ] Identify openly distributable PDFs, figures, and other useful assets; flag materials requiring user-provided copies.
- [ ] Add unconventional and obscure research leads with explicit evidence and uncertainty labels.

### Review and maintenance

- [ ] Check links, source metadata, and grade consistency.
- [ ] Record collection and review activity in `log.md`.
- [ ] Keep the index usable as the vault expands; add links to new material as it is created.

## Research log

Treat `log.md` as append-only: add every entry at the end with an ISO 8601 timestamp and timezone; never edit or delete previous entries. Record areas reviewed, sources added, structural/grading decisions, blockers, corrections (as new entries), and next steps. Keep this checklist updated alongside the log.

*** Update File: Research/Research/Statistical testing pitfalls.md
@@
 ## Base rates and low prior probability
@@
 When true tradable edges are rare and many claims are tested, even apparently strong nominal significance may produce a low probability that a new result is real. Prior evidence, economic mechanism, independent replication, and realistic costs matter.
+
+As a simple illustration, if only 1% of tested ideas are genuinely useful and a procedure has 5% false-positive rate and 80% power, then among 10,000 tested ideas there are about 100 true positives (80 detected) and 9,900 nulls (495 false positives). Only about 14% of positive results would be true under those assumptions. The numbers are illustrative and assume a simple common test; actual financial search is more complex, but the base-rate lesson remains.
*** End Patch

1: # Official and Vendor Alternative-Data Source Notes
2: 
3: This source note distinguishes a data publisher's documented product from a claim that the data is complete or predictive.
4: 
5: ## EIA Open Data
6: 
7: - **Type:** U.S. government statistical agency, energy API and bulk downloads.
8: - **Docs:** [Open Data](https://www.eia.gov/opendata/) · [Weekly Petroleum Status Report](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/)
9: - **Grade:** 1 for agency documentation and issued observations; series-level methods/latency still vary.
10: - **Useful:** Weekly inventory/balance and import/export tables, natural gas storage, power load/generation, prices, outages, projections.
11: - **Access:** API registration/key; terms and reuse policy linked by EIA. Bulk files are listed and EIA documents a twice-daily update process.
12: - **Caveats:** Survey estimates, preliminary/final status, changing report tables, rounding, revision and release schedule. Keep release vintage; distinguish projection from realized data.
13: 
14: ## NOAA NCEI Climate Data Online
15: 
16: - **Type:** U.S. government climate archive and web-service API.
17: - **Docs:** [CDO Web Services v2](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/webservices/v2)
18: - **Grade:** 1 for service descriptions and published station observations.
19: - **Access:** API token; official docs state 5 requests/second and 10,000 requests/day per token. Data endpoint has date-span and pagination limits.
20: - **Caveats:** Station relocation, equipment changes, reporting latency, missingness, quality flags, aggregation/unit choices, and data revisions. Model local weather/exposure, not just nearest-station readings.
21: 
22: ## U.S. Census International Trade API
23: 
24: - **Type:** U.S. government trade statistics.
25: - **Docs:** [International Trade datasets](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/international-trade.html)
26: - **Grade:** 1 for published data and methodological descriptions.
27: - **Timing/versioning:** Monthly series from January 2010 to present, updated on release day; Census says previously released monthly trade data are revised annually with April statistics.
28: - **Access:** API key now required per page; endpoints permit product/country/district/state/port classification queries.
29: - **Caveats:** Monthly publication lag, annual revision, classification changes, confidentiality suppression, valuation and quantity definitions. Release date is the information time; reference month is not.
30: 
31: ## EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (WPSR)
32: 
33: - **Type:** EIA weekly energy market report with CSV/XLS/PDF tables and archives.
34: - **Docs:** [WPSR](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/)
35: - **Grade:** 1 for EIA's own report and methodology.
36: - **Useful tables:** Petroleum balance, refinery inputs/production, stocks, imports/exports, preliminary crude imports, and estimates.
37: - **Caveats:** Release clock and holiday shifts; totals may not exactly sum due to independent rounding. EIA posts notices when tables are discontinued or changed; report pages also include errata and methodology. Avoid scraping a current table as if its structure was constant.
38: 
39: ## MarineTraffic / Kpler maritime intelligence
40: 
41: - **Type:** Commercial maritime AIS and event/derived-data product.
42: - **Docs:** [MarineTraffic Data Services](https://www.marinetraffic.com/en/ais-api-services) · [Kpler developer portal](https://developers.kpler.com/)
43: - **Grade:** 5 for provider's own coverage and service claims; independently test empirical completeness.
44: - **Advertised product areas:** Real-time AIS, historical tracks (page claims archive since 2010), vessel database, port/operational events, and predictive ETA/destination products.
45: - **Access:** Commercial service / request-demo path; developer documentation and terms govern use. No open unlimited full-history download established by reviewed page.
46: - **Caveats:** Terrestrial/satellite reception coverage, transmission gaps, identity resolution, AIS spoofing/manipulation, inferred cargo/destination, backfills, model-generated event labels, and changing receiver network. Retrospective predictions may not equal the forecast that existed at the time.
47: 
48: ## Source-use principle
49: 
50: For each source, keep provider documentation as a primary source about product behavior and a lower-grade source about completeness or alpha. Preserve raw inputs, query/version, release/receipt time, terms, and separate model-derived fields from direct measurements.

- **Useful:** Weekly inventory/balance and import/export tables, natural gas storage, power load/generation, prices, outages, projections.
- **Access:** API registration/key; terms and reuse policy linked by EIA. Bulk files are listed and EIA documents a twice-daily update process.
- **Caveats:** Survey estimates, preliminary/final status, changing report tables, rounding, revision and release schedule. Keep release vintage; distinguish projection from realized data.

## NOAA NCEI Climate Data Online

- **Type:** U.S. government climate archive and web-service API.
- **Docs:** [CDO Web Services v2](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/webservices/v2)
- **Grade:** 1 for service descriptions and published station observations.
- **Access:** API token; official docs state 5 requests/second and 10,000 requests/day per token. Data endpoint has date-span and pagination limits.
- **Caveats:** Station relocation, equipment changes, reporting latency, missingness, quality flags, aggregation/unit choices, and data revisions. Model local weather/exposure, not just nearest-station readings.

## U.S. Census International Trade API

- **Type:** U.S. government trade statistics.
- **Docs:** [International Trade datasets](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/international-trade.html)
- **Grade:** 1 for published data and methodological descriptions.
- **Timing/versioning:** Monthly series from January 2010 to present, updated on release day; Census says previously released monthly trade data are revised annually with April statistics.
- **Access:** API key now required per page; endpoints permit product/country/district/state/port classification queries.
- **Caveats:** Monthly publication lag, annual revision, classification changes, confidentiality suppression, valuation and quantity definitions. Release date is the information time; reference month is not.

## EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (WPSR)

- **Type:** EIA weekly energy market report with CSV/XLS/PDF tables and archives.
- **Docs:** [WPSR](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/)
- **Grade:** 1 for EIA's own report and methodology.
- **Useful tables:** Petroleum balance, refinery inputs/production, stocks, imports/exports, preliminary crude imports, and estimates.
- **Caveats:** Release clock and holiday shifts; totals may not exactly sum due to independent rounding. EIA posts notices when tables are discontinued or changed; report pages also include errata and methodology. Avoid scraping a current table as if its structure was constant.

## MarineTraffic / Kpler maritime intelligence

- **Type:** Commercial maritime AIS and event/derived-data product.
- **Docs:** [MarineTraffic Data Services](https://www.marinetraffic.com/en/ais-api-services) · [Kpler developer portal](https://developers.kpler.com/)
- **Grade:** 5 for provider's own coverage and service claims; independently test empirical completeness.
- **Advertised product areas:** Real-time AIS, historical tracks (page claims archive since 2010), vessel database, port/operational events, and predictive ETA/destination products.
- **Access:** Commercial service / request-demo path; developer documentation and terms govern use. No open unlimited full-history download established by reviewed page.
- **Caveats:** Terrestrial/satellite reception coverage, transmission gaps, identity resolution, AIS spoofing/manipulation, inferred cargo/destination, backfills, model-generated event labels, and changing receiver network. Retrospective predictions may not equal the forecast that existed at the time.

## Source-use principle

For each source, keep provider documentation as a primary source about product behavior and a lower-grade source about completeness or alpha. Preserve raw inputs, query/version, release/receipt time, terms, and separate model-derived fields from direct measurements.

+# Reading Access and Local Assets
+
+This inventory distinguishes material that can be read online from files that are clearly licensed for local redistribution. A public URL or downloadable PDF does **not** by itself establish permission to copy it into the vault. Link to sources by default; download only where the license/terms explicitly allow the intended use.
+
+## Open online material
+
+- [[Sources/Forecasting Principles and Practice]] — Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*, third edition; free online textbook at [OTexts](https://otexts.com/fpp3/). The source note links the online text; no local copy is required.
+- [[Sources/Athey Imbens 2017]] — academic review/preprint with an [arXiv abstract and PDF](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00699). Verify the current arXiv license before saving a local copy or figures.
+- [[Sources/Bacry Mastromatteo Muzy 2015]] — academic review/preprint with [arXiv abstract and PDF](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04592). Verify license for local redistribution.
+- [[Sources/Rolnick et al 2019]] — climate/ML review with an [arXiv page](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05433); link and summarize, and confirm license before local copying.
+- [[Sources/Harvey Liu Zhu 2016]], [[Sources/Novy-Marx 2015]], [[Sources/Diebold Mariano 1995]], [[Sources/Moreira Muir 2017]], [[Sources/Obizhaeva Wang 2005]], and other academic sources link to publisher/repository/NBER records. Availability of a working-paper PDF does not automatically authorize local distribution.
+
+## User-provided or permission-dependent
+
+- Marcos López de Prado, *Advances in Financial Machine Learning* — copyrighted book; see [[Sources/Financial ML field notes]]. Obtain via a lawful library/publisher copy; provide a copy only if licensed for this use.
+- Cboe methodology/product PDFs and historical data — see [[Sources/Cboe VIX methodology and data]]. The source pages link official materials, but current terms govern retention and reuse; no local copies included.
+- Cboe/NBER/publisher working papers, exchange feed documentation, commercial datasets, and vendor reports — link and summarize unless an explicit license permits the specific local use and redistribution.
+- London Strategic Edge data — SDK and data terms are distinct; provider terms restrict redistribution. The SDK itself is MIT-licensed, but that does not license downloaded market data. See [[Data/London Strategic Edge]] and [[Sources/LSE data SDK]].
+
+## Figures and diagrams
+
+No third-party figures were copied into the vault in this pass. For educational diagrams, prefer creating original schematics (e.g., point-in-time data lineage, contract roll timeline, or option payoff) and label them as original illustrations. If reproducing a published figure, record author, source, exact license/permission, and modifications in a nearby caption.
+
+## Maintenance rule
+
+Before adding any PDF/image locally, record its source URL, author, publication/version, license/permission, retrieval date, and intended audience/use. If these are unclear, retain a link and summary rather than copying the file.
+
+Related: [[Source grading]] · [[Source note template]] · [[Research workflow]] · [[Data provenance and point-in-time]]
*** End Patch

*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: Research/Mathematics/Portfolio construction and estimation risk.md
+# Portfolio Construction and Estimation Risk
+
+Portfolio construction maps forecasts and risk estimates into weights. The optimizer is only as credible as its inputs, constraints, cost model, and point-in-time universe.
+
+## Mean-variance setup
+
+For expected excess returns \(\mu\), covariance \(\Sigma\), weights \(w\), and risk-aversion \(\lambda>0\), a basic objective is
+
+\[
+\max_w\; \mu^Tw-\frac{\lambda}{2}w^T\Sigma w
+\quad\text{subject to }\mathbf{1}^Tw=1.
+\]
+
+Without further constraints and for positive-definite \(\Sigma\), the solution is
+
+\[
+w=\frac{1}{\lambda}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\nu\mathbf{1}),\qquad
+\nu=\frac{\mathbf{1}^T\Sigma^{-1}\mu-\lambda}{\mathbf{1}^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}}.
+\]
+
+The inverse covariance amplifies estimation noise in low-variance directions. If the estimated returns are small relative to their uncertainty, optimizer weights can become extreme and unstable. Constraints (long-only, leverage, sector, turnover, liquidity) change the solution and must be recorded as part of the strategy.
+
+## Worked intuition: two assets
+
+For two assets with equal expected returns and equal variance, positive correlation reduces diversification benefit; the unconstrained minimum-variance portfolio is symmetric. If the estimated correlation falls slightly below zero, the optimizer may assign concentrated or offsetting positions. With finite data, that small sign change may be estimation noise. Compare weights under a range of covariance estimates and use shrinkage or robust constraints; judge stability and realized net outcomes, not just in-sample variance.
+
+## Turnover-aware objective
+
+A practical objective can penalize trading from current weights \(w_0\):
+
+\[
+\max_w\; \mu^Tw-\frac{\lambda}{2}w^T\Sigma w-C(w-w_0),
+\]
+
+where \(C\) may include linear spread/fees and nonlinear impact/borrow estimates. Cost estimates are uncertain and endogenous to liquidity. Rebalance timing, partial fills, and binding constraints can make actual exposure differ from target weights; evaluate realized holdings and costs.
+
+## Robustness protocol
+
+1. Estimate \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) using only the training window; document horizons and units.
+2. Compare equal-weight, minimum-variance, benchmark, and forecast-driven allocations.
+3. Perturb expected returns/covariances within plausible estimation uncertainty and record weight sensitivity.
+4. Enforce gross/net leverage, concentration, sector, liquidity, borrow, and turnover constraints.
+5. Include fees, spreads, financing, market impact, and a capacity curve.
+6. Evaluate weights on chronological out-of-sample data; report realized risk, returns, drawdown/tails, turnover, exposures, and constraint breaches.
+
+## Sources and evidence
+
+- **Harry Markowitz (1952), “Portfolio Selection,” *The Journal of Finance*.** Grade 2 for the foundational mean-variance framework; recency: foundational; novelty: foundational; source type: peer-reviewed theory paper. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x). Limitation: the model assumes inputs and constraints that are difficult to estimate/implement; it does not establish realized strategy performance.
+- **Olivier Ledoit & Michael Wolf (2004), “Honey, I Shrunk the Sample Covariance Matrix,” *The Journal of Portfolio Management*.** Grade 2 for covariance shrinkage methodology; recency: foundational; novelty: established estimation technique; source type: peer-reviewed methods paper. [Author-hosted paper](https://www.ledoit.net/honey.pdf). Limitation: shrinkage improves estimation under its setup, but does not guarantee optimal portfolio utility in every market or with arbitrary costs.
+
+## Exercise
+
+Using a small point-in-time asset universe, compare equal-weight, sample-covariance minimum variance, and one pre-specified shrinkage portfolio. Use expanding chronological estimation; report turnover, max weight, realized volatility, and net performance. Add a small perturbation to each mean/covariance input and quantify weight sensitivity. State whether any result is a forecasting claim, a risk-allocation result, or neither.
+
+Related: [[Convexity and constrained optimization]] · [[Regression covariance and PCA]] · [[Edge validation]] · [[Execution cost validation protocol]] · [[Overfitting controls]]
*** End Patch

Parameters


api_key
Read API Keys for more information.
32 character alpha-numeric lowercase string, required


file_type
A key or file extension that indicates the type of file to send.
string, optional, default: xml
One of the following values: 'xml', 'json', 'xlsx', 'csv'

xml = Extensible Markup Language
json = JavaScript Object Notation
xlsx = Excel Spreadsheet
csv = Comma-Separated Values Text Format (File is returned as compressed zip file. The zip file contains the specified file format csv and a text README file.)




series_id
The id for a series.
string, required


realtime_start
The start of the real-time period.  For more information, see Real-Time Periods, vintage_dates.
YYYY-MM-DD formatted string, optional, default: today's date


realtime_end
The end of the real-time period.  For more information, see Real-Time Periods, vintage_dates.
YYYY-MM-DD formatted string, optional, default: today's date


limit
The maximum number of results to return.
integer between 1 and 100000, optional, default: 100000


offset
non-negative integer, optional, default: 0


sort_order
Sort results is ascending or descending observation_date order.
One of the following strings: 'asc', 'desc'.
optional, default: asc


observation_start
The start of the observation period.
YYYY-MM-DD formatted string, optional, default: 1776-07-04 (earliest available)


observation_end
The end of the observation period.
YYYY-MM-DD formatted string, optional, default: 9999-12-31 (latest available)


units
A key that indicates a data value transformation.
string, optional, default: lin (No transformation)
One of the following values: 'lin', 'chg', 'ch1', 'pch', 'pc1', 'pca', 'cch', 'cca', 'log'

lin = Levels (No transformation)
chg = Change
ch1 = Change from Year Ago             
pch = Percent Change
pc1 = Percent Change from Year Ago             
pca = Compounded Annual Rate of Change
cch = Continuously Compounded Rate of Change
cca = Continuously Compounded Annual Rate of Change
log = Natural Log

For unit transformation formulas, see:

https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/help#growth_formulas



frequency

An optional parameter that indicates a lower frequency to aggregate values to.  
The FRED frequency aggregation feature converts higher frequency data series into lower frequency data series (e.g. converts a monthly data series into an annual data series). 
In FRED, the highest frequency data is daily, and the lowest frequency data is annual.   
There are 3 aggregation methods available- average, sum, and end of period.  
See the aggregation_method parameter. 

string, optional, default: no value for no frequency aggregation
One of the following values: 'd', 'w', 'bw', 'm', 'q', 'sa', 'a', 'wef', 'weth', 'wew', 'wetu', 'wem', 'wesu', 'wesa', 'bwew', 'bwem'


Frequencies without period descriptions:

d = Daily
w = Weekly
bw = Biweekly
m = Monthly
q = Quarterly
sa = Semiannual
a = Annual




Frequencies with period descriptions:

wef = Weekly, Ending Friday
weth = Weekly, Ending Thursday
wew = Weekly, Ending Wednesday
wetu = Weekly, Ending Tuesday
wem = Weekly, Ending Monday
wesu = Weekly, Ending Sunday
wesa = Weekly, Ending Saturday
bwew = Biweekly, Ending Wednesday
bwem = Biweekly, Ending Monday





    Note that an error will be returned if a frequency is specified that is higher than the native frequency of the series.
    For instance if a series has the native frequency 'Monthly' (as returned by the fred/series request), 
    it is not possible to aggregate the series to the higher 'Daily' frequency using the frequency parameter value 'd'. 



    No frequency aggregation will occur if the frequency specified by the frequency parameter matches the native frequency of the series.  
    For instance if the value of the frequency parameter is 'm' and the native frequency of the series is 'Monthly' (as returned by the fred/series request), 
    observations will be returned, but they will not be aggregated to a lower frequency. 



    For most cases, it will be sufficient to specify a lower frequency without a period description (e.g. 'd', 'w', 'bw', 'm', 'q', 'sa', 'a') as opposed to frequencies with period descriptions 
    (e.g. 'wef', 'weth', 'wew', 'wetu', 'wem', 'wesu', 'wesa', 'bwew', 'bwem') which only exist for the weekly and biweekly frequencies.  
        
        
            The weekly and biweekly frequencies with periods exist to offer more options and override the default periods implied by values 'w' and 'bw'.
        
        
            The value 'w' defaults to frequency and period 'Weekly, Ending Friday' when aggregating daily series.
        
        
            The value 'bw' defaults to frequency and period 'Biweekly, Ending Wednesday' when aggregating daily and weekly series.
        
        
            Consider the difference between values 'w' for 'Weekly' and 'wef' for 'Weekly, Ending Friday'.    
            When aggregating observations from daily to weekly, the value 'w' defaults to frequency and period 'Weekly, Ending Friday' which is the same as 'wef'.   
            Here, the difference is that the period 'Ending Friday' is implicit for value 'w' but explicit for value 'wef'.
            However, if a series has native frequency 'Weekly, Ending Monday', an error will be returned for value 'wef' but not value 'w'.
        
    



    Note that frequency aggregation is currently only available for file_type equal to xml or json due to time constraints.


    Read the 'Frequency Aggregation' section of the FRED FAQs 
    for implementation details.




aggregation_method

A key that indicates the aggregation method used for frequency aggregation.  
This parameter has no affect if the frequency parameter is not set. 

string, optional, default: avg
One of the following values: 'avg', 'sum', 'eop'


avg = Average
sum = Sum
eop = End of Period





output_type
An integer that indicates an output type.
integer, optional, default: 1
One of the following values: '1', '2', '3', '4'
 
1 = Observations by Real-Time Period 
2 = Observations by Vintage Date, All Observations 
3 = Observations by Vintage Date, New and Revised Observations Only 
4 = Observations, Initial Release Only  


For output types '2' and '3', some XML attribute names start with the series ID which may have a first character that is a number (i.e. 0 through 9).  
In this case only, the XML attribute name starts with an underscore then the series ID in order to avoid invalid XML.  
If the series ID starts with a letter (i.e. A through Z) then an underscore is not prepended.


For more information, read:

https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/help/downloaddata#outputformats



vintage_dates
A comma separated string of YYYY-MM-DD formatted dates in history (e.g. 2000-01-01,2005-02-24).
Vintage dates are used to download data as it existed on these specified dates in history.
Vintage dates can be specified instead of a real-time period using realtime_start and realtime_end.

Sometimes it may be useful to enter a vintage date that is not a date when the data values were revised. 
For instance you may want to know the latest available revisions on a particular date.
Entering a vintage date is also useful to compare series on different releases with different release dates.
    string, optional, no vintage dates are set by default. 

    Your query will be limited to a specific number of vintage dates depending on the series_id, file_type and output_type specified.
    
        output_type=2, series_id=USRECD: 110 csv, 55 xlsx
        output_type=2, any daily series: 450 csv, 225 xlsx
        any output_type or other series: 1000 csv, 1000 xlsx, 2000 json, 2000 xml

State space modeling: Local Linear Trends#
This notebook describes how to extend the statsmodels statespace classes to create and estimate a custom model. Here we develop a local linear trend model.
The Local Linear Trend model has the form (see Durbin and Koopman 2012, Chapter 3.2 for all notation and details):

\[\begin{split}\begin{align}
y_t & = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t \qquad & \varepsilon_t \sim
    N(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2) \\
\mu_{t+1} & = \mu_t + \nu_t + \xi_t & \xi_t \sim N(0, \sigma_\xi^2) \\
\nu_{t+1} & = \nu_t + \zeta_t & \zeta_t \sim N(0, \sigma_\zeta^2)
\end{align}\end{split}\]
It is easy to see that this can be cast into state space form as:

\[\begin{split}\begin{align}
y_t & = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t \\ \nu_t \end{pmatrix} + \varepsilon_t \\
\begin{pmatrix} \mu_{t+1} \\ \nu_{t+1} \end{pmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t \\ \nu_t \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \xi_t \\ \zeta_t \end{pmatrix}
\end{align}\end{split}\]
Notice that much of the state space representation is composed of known values; in fact the only parts in which parameters to be estimated appear are in the variance / covariance matrices:

\[\begin{split}\begin{align}
H_t & = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \end{bmatrix} \\
Q_t & = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_\xi^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_\zeta^2 \end{bmatrix}
\end{align}\end{split}\]

[1]:


%matplotlib inline

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import statsmodels.api as sm



To take advantage of the existing infrastructure, including Kalman filtering and maximum likelihood estimation, we create a new class which extends from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.MLEModel. There are a number of things that must be specified:

k_states, k_posdef: These two parameters must be provided to the base classes in initialization. The inform the statespace model about the size of, respectively, the state vector, above \(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_t & \nu_t \end{pmatrix}'\), and the state error vector, above \(\begin{pmatrix} \xi_t & \zeta_t \end{pmatrix}'\). Note that the dimension of the endogenous vector does not have to be specified, since it can be inferred from the endog array.
update: The method update, with argument params, must be specified (it is used when fit() is called to calculate the MLE). It takes the parameters and fills them into the appropriate state space matrices. For example, below, the params vector contains variance parameters \(\begin{pmatrix} \sigma_\varepsilon^2 & \sigma_\xi^2 & \sigma_\zeta^2\end{pmatrix}\), and the update method must place them in the observation and state covariance matrices. More generally, the
parameter vector might be mapped into many different places in all of the statespace matrices.
statespace matrices: by default, all state space matrices (obs_intercept, design, obs_cov, state_intercept, transition, selection, state_cov) are set to zeros. Values that are fixed (like the ones in the design and transition matrices here) can be set in initialization, whereas values that vary with the parameters should be set in the update method. Note that it is easy to forget to set the selection matrix, which is often just the identity matrix (as it is here), but not setting
it will lead to a very different model (one where there is not a stochastic component to the transition equation).
start params: start parameters must be set, even if it is just a vector of zeros, although often good start parameters can be found from the data. Maximum likelihood estimation by gradient methods (as employed here) can be sensitive to the starting parameters, so it is important to select good ones if possible. Here it does not matter too much (although as variances, they should’t be set zero).
initialization: in addition to defined state space matrices, all state space models must be initialized with the mean and variance for the initial distribution of the state vector. If the distribution is known, initialize_known(initial_state, initial_state_cov) can be called, or if the model is stationary (e.g. an ARMA model), initialize_stationary can be used. Otherwise, initialize_approximate_diffuse is a reasonable generic initialization (exact diffuse initialization is not
yet available). Since the local linear trend model is not stationary (it is composed of random walks) and since the distribution is not generally known, we use initialize_approximate_diffuse below.

The above are the minimum necessary for a successful model. There are also a number of things that do not have to be set, but which may be helpful or important for some applications:

transform / untransform: when fit is called, the optimizer in the background will use gradient methods to select the parameters that maximize the likelihood function. By default it uses unbounded optimization, which means that it may select any parameter value. In many cases, that is not the desired behavior; variances, for example, cannot be negative. To get around this, the transform method takes the unconstrained vector of parameters provided by the optimizer and returns a
constrained vector of parameters used in likelihood evaluation. untransform provides the reverse operation.
param_names: this internal method can be used to set names for the estimated parameters so that e.g. the summary provides meaningful names. If not present, parameters are named param0, param1, etc.


[2]:


"""
Univariate Local Linear Trend Model
"""


class LocalLinearTrend(sm.tsa.statespace.MLEModel):
    def __init__(self, endog):
        # Model order
        k_states = k_posdef = 2

        # Initialize the statespace
        super().__init__(
            endog,
            k_states=k_states,
            k_posdef=k_posdef,
            initialization="approximate_diffuse",
            loglikelihood_burn=k_states,
        )

        # Initialize the matrices
        self.ssm["design"] = np.array([1, 0])
        self.ssm["transition"] = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 1]])
        self.ssm["selection"] = np.eye(k_states)

        # Cache some indices
        self._state_cov_idx = ("state_cov",) + np.diag_indices(k_posdef)

    @property
    def param_names(self):
        return ["sigma2.measurement", "sigma2.level", "sigma2.trend"]

    @property
    def start_params(self):
        return [np.std(self.endog)] * 3

    def transform_params(self, unconstrained):
        return unconstrained**2

    def untransform_params(self, constrained):
        return constrained**0.5

    def update(self, params, *args, **kwargs):
        params = super().update(params, *args, **kwargs)

        # Observation covariance
        self.ssm["obs_cov", 0, 0] = params[0]

        # State covariance
        self.ssm[self._state_cov_idx] = params[1:]



Using this simple model, we can estimate the parameters from a local linear trend model. The following example is from Commandeur and Koopman (2007), section 3.4., modeling motor vehicle fatalities in Finland.

[3]:


# Download the dataset
df = pd.read_table(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/statsmodels/smdatasets/refs/heads/main/data/statespace-local-linear-trend/NorwayFinland.txt",
    skiprows=1,
    header=None,
    sep=r"\s+",
    engine="python",
    names=["date", "nf", "ff"],
)



Since we defined the local linear trend model as extending from MLEModel, the fit() method is immediately available, just as in other statsmodels maximum likelihood classes. Similarly, the returned results class supports many of the same post-estimation results, like the summary method.

[4]:


# Load Dataset
df.index = pd.date_range(
    start=f"{df.date[0]}-01-01", end=f"{df.iloc[-1, 0]}-01-01", freq="YS"
)

# Log transform
df["lff"] = np.log(df["ff"])

# Setup the model
mod = LocalLinearTrend(df["lff"])

# Fit it using MLE (recall that we are fitting the three variance parameters)
res = mod.fit(disp=False)
print(res.summary())

Finally, we can do post-estimation prediction and forecasting. Notice that the end period can be specified as a date.

[5]:


# Perform prediction and forecasting
predict = res.get_prediction()
forecast = res.get_forecast("2014")




[6]:


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))

# Plot the results
df["lff"].plot(ax=ax, style="k.", label="Observations")
predict.predicted_mean.plot(ax=ax, label="One-step-ahead Prediction")
predict_ci = predict.conf_int(alpha=0.05)
predict_index = np.arange(len(predict_ci))
ax.fill_between(
    predict_index[2:], predict_ci.iloc[2:, 0], predict_ci.iloc[2:, 1], alpha=0.1
)

forecast.predicted_mean.plot(ax=ax, style="r", label="Forecast")
forecast_ci = forecast.conf_int()
forecast_index = np.arange(len(predict_ci), len(predict_ci) + len(forecast_ci))
ax.fill_between(
    forecast_index, forecast_ci.iloc[:, 0], forecast_ci.iloc[:, 1], alpha=0.1
)

# Cleanup the image
ax.set_ylim((4, 8))
legend = ax.legend(loc="lower left");

| Weather and climate | Temperature anomalies, precipitation, storm tracks, drought | Agriculture, power, gas, insurance, shipping | Station coverage, forecast vs realized weather, spatial aggregation, seasonality, revisions |

| Shipping / AIS | Vessel positions, port calls, draught, destination, ship-to-ship events | Energy, dry bulk, agriculture, freight, insurers | Satellite/receiver coverage, spoofing, identity resolution, missing transmissions, destination inference |
| Satellite / remote sensing | Night lights, crop conditions, inventories, industrial activity | Agriculture, metals, energy, regional growth | Cloud/observation gaps, processing revisions, proprietary transformations, proxy ambiguity |
| Public filings / text | SEC filings, earnings transcripts, policy releases, court/regulatory documents | Equities, credit, rates, FX, sector baskets | Publication/acceptance time, amendments, parsing quality, selection and text-model leakage |
| Consumer / digital activity | Search interest, app usage, web prices, job postings, reviews | Consumer equities, inflation, labor, retail, travel | Platform coverage, bots, sample selection, backfills, API changes, licensing/privacy |
| Policy / geopolitical events | Sanctions, trade restrictions, elections, conflict, regulation | Country exposures, FX, commodities, credit, sector/issuer spreads | Event date ambiguity, anticipation, narrative coding, concurrent news, subjective classification |

## Evidence scale and acquisition status

- **Official source data:** EIA, NOAA NCEI, U.S. Census, SEC EDGAR, CFTC, and statistical agencies; often Grade 1–2 for what they publish, but still require timing, revisions, and construction checks.
- **Primary private/vendor feeds:** maritime AIS products and commercial alternative datasets; typically Grade 5 for vendor feature claims until coverage/completeness are independently assessed.
- **Articles, reports, stories:** good for hypothesis discovery, not proof; grade the specific claim separately.

## Source leads with reviewed documentation

- [[Financial data source directory]] covers EIA, NOAA, Census trade, SEC, CFTC, BIS, and relevant access notes.
- EIA's [Weekly Petroleum Status Report](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/) provides weekly balance, inventory, imports/exports and other tables with release materials and prior issues. EIA documentation notes tables and methodology can change; preserve report vintage and release timestamp.
- Census [Monthly International Trade](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/international-trade.html) is available from January 2010 onward and is revised annually with April statistics. Preserve release vintages and commodity classifications.
- NOAA [Climate Data Online API](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/webservices/v2) provides station and dataset metadata plus observations; an API token is required and rate limits apply.
- MarineTraffic/Kpler [data services](https://www.marinetraffic.com/en/ais-api-services) advertise live/past AIS, port events, and vessel records, with commercial access/demo inquiry. Treat coverage and predictive-event products as vendor claims; validate independently. AIS observations are not complete global vessel truth.
- [[Sources/Fisman Hamao Wang 2014]] is an academic example of testing an unusual political-exposure channel using defined events and firm-level exposure.
- [[Sources/Rolnick et al 2019]] is a broad ML/climate application map, not evidence of market return prediction.

## Build a lead hypothesis before querying

Write: **mechanism → measurement → availability → exposed market → test → falsifier.** For example, a potential port disruption might affect a grade/location-specific commodity curve only after vessel congestion is observable, with a lead determined by transit and inventory buffers. Name a placebo port or unrelated contract the mechanism should not affect.

# Quantitative Research Obsidian Vault — Plan

> **Vault folder:** `Research` (Obsidian vault name: `research`)

## Purpose

Build a deep, linked educational and research vault for interns learning to develop, research, and test ideas. The broad scope includes economics and quantitative methods, with the primary emphasis on quantifying data, identifying statistically credible market edges, and understanding how edges may decay.

Collect a wide range of material, including less conventional or obscure leads. Preserve the distinction between a novel hypothesis and evidence that supports it: unusual correlations may inspire research, but must be labeled and tested rather than presented as established alpha.

## Source and evidence policy

- Search broadly across academic research, textbooks, lecture notes, technical writing, datasets, and documented practitioner accounts.
- Classify source claims on a **1–10 evidence/provenance scale** (lower is stronger). Grade 1 is a recent, reputable peer-reviewed/academic or primary-source item with transparent methodology, accessible provenance, and independently checkable evidence. Grades 2–3 are strong academic/official sources with minor caveats or early-stage status; grades 4–6 are useful but more limited, older, indirect, or methodologically incomplete; grades 7–8 are trade/practitioner and secondary material with partial verification; grades 9–10 are anecdotal stories, opaque claims, or unverified leads. The grade applies to the source's support for a specific claim, not to whether the idea deserves exploration.
- Keep **evidence grade**, **recency**, and **novelty** as separate fields. A dated foundational result may remain high-quality evidence; a recent vendor claim is not high-quality evidence simply because it is current.
- Record publication/update date, author or institution, source type, methods, limitations, and a direct link wherever available.
- Treat recency and reliability as separate considerations: an older foundational result can remain valuable, and a recent anecdote is not strong evidence merely because it is recent.
- Summarize and link copyrighted works. Include local copies only when distribution is permitted. Flag useful works that require the user to provide a copy.
- Include a practical London Strategic Edge data-source walkthrough, verifying access requirements, dependencies, data formats, quotas, and workflow against current official documentation and repository source.

## Vault structure

Create a navigable `index.md` and a running `log.md`, then organize substantial subject areas into linked topic notes and subtopics. Keep market-specific material in dedicated folders and cross-link it to shared methods and concepts.

### Core areas to cover

- Mathematics: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, probability, statistics, optimization, and multidimensional geometry/topology.
- Econometrics and economics: time series, causal inference, forecasting, market and macroeconomic data, and empirical methods.
- Machine learning: supervised and unsupervised learning, deep learning, LSTMs and sequence methods, reinforcement learning, and applications to financial data.
- Research practice: data quality, feature construction, backtesting, validation, multiple testing, leakage, overfitting prevention, statistical significance, robustness, and edge decay.
- Engineering: efficient data workflows, profiling, runtime reduction, code execution and numerical optimization, reproducibility, and research pipelines.
- Data and alternative hypotheses: document provenance, transformations, limitations, and evidence quality; retain unconventional leads with clear uncertainty labels.

### Market folders

Create dedicated folders for at least:

- Forex
- ETFs
- Crypto
- Equities
- Futures
- Options
- Fixed income
- Commodities

Add further markets when useful. Each market area should cover relevant data, instruments, market structure, research considerations, and links to shared methods.

- [x] Add a primary financial/economic data-source directory and detailed point-in-time, vintage, identifier, revision, and access guidance.
- [x] Add an alternative-data opportunity map, physical-supply-chain case study, source notes, and an evaluation checklist.
- [x] Add practical ingestion architecture, schema validation, experiment tracking, and reproducibility guidance.
- [x] Deepen time-series research with forecast comparison, structural instability, volatility forecasting, and a practical stability exercise.

33: - **Direct verified URLs:** [Bulk downloads](https://data.bis.org/bulkdownload) · [API documentation](https://stats.bis.org/api-doc/v2/) · [permitted-use terms](https://data.bis.org/help/legal#terms-of-permitted-use-of-bis-statistics).

35: - **Access/timing/terms:** Public downloads/API without an access key in the reviewed docs. 36: - **Limitations:** Aggregates and estimates compiled from national sources, variable coverage/frequency, revisions and breaks; derivatives statistics are not contract-level quotes/trades. Bulk files are snapshots, so archive downloaded file/version and retrieval timestamp for vintage control.
37: - **Assessment:** Grade 1 for published metadata/access; recent 2026-10-18; novelty moderate (specific ready-to-download formats/update dates). Source type: international organization primary statistical compilation.

39: ## Public exchange and regulator data: bars, histories, reference data
40: 
41: ### CFTC Commitments of Traders (COT) — positioning, not price
42: 
43: - **Direct verified URLs:** [COT hub and report definitions](https://www.cftc.gov/MarketReports/CommitmentsofTraders/index.htm) · [Public Reporting Environment](https://publicreporting.cftc.gov/) · [release schedule](https://www.cftc.gov/MarketReports/CommitmentsofTraders/ReleaseSchedule/index.htm).

58: 
59: - **Direct verified URLs:** [U.S. market data products](https://www.nasdaq.com/products/data) · [public stock screener](https://www.nasdaq.com/market-activity/stocks/screener) · [Nasdaq options chain page](https://www.nasdaq.com/market-activity/quotes/option-chain).

66: 
67: - **Direct verified URLs:** [OCC market data and reports](https://www.theocc.com/market-data) · [OCC data products](https://www.theocc.com/market-data/market-data-reports).

76: 
77: - **Direct verified URLs:** [REST OHLC endpoint](https://docs.kraken.com/api/docs/rest-api/get-ohlc-data) · [WebSocket v2 market data](https://docs.kraken.com/api/docs/websocket-v2/ticker) · [API overview](https://docs.kraken.com/api/).

79: - **Access/timing/terms:** Public endpoints generally require no key for public market data; private account/trade actions require credentials.
